claim: MDGA1 antiserum recognizes recombinant HA-MDGA1 as a 130 kDa band on immunoblots.
source: The MDGA1 antiserum recognized recombinant HA-MDGA1 (but not HA-MDGA2) extracted from HEK-293T cells as a 130 kDa band on immunoblots (Figure 1A), above the molecular weight of 101 kDa expected from the amino-acid sequence, suggesting glycosylation of the protein i.e. through the addition of N-linked sugar chains.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text, demonstrating the molecular weight of MDGA1 detected by the antiserum.

claim: The MDGA1 antiserum does not recognize HA-MDGA2.
source: The MDGA1 antiserum recognized recombinant HA-MDGA1 (but not HA-MDGA2) extracted from HEK-293T cells as a 130 kDa band on immunoblots (Figure 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating specificity of the MDGA1 antiserum.

claim: The molecular weight of MDGA1 detected by immunoblot (130 kDa) is above the expected molecular weight from the amino-acid sequence (101 kDa), suggesting glycosylation.
source: The MDGA1 antiserum recognized recombinant HA-MDGA1 (but not HA-MDGA2) extracted from HEK-293T cells as a 130 kDa band on immunoblots (Figure 1A), above the molecular weight of 101 kDa expected from the amino-acid sequence, suggesting glycosylation of the protein i.e. through the addition of N-linked sugar chains.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed molecular weight difference between detected and predicted values.

claim: The reactivity of MDGA1 antiserum to MDGA1 was abolished by pre-incubation with excess recombinant MDGA1-Fc antigen.
source: The reactivity to MDGA1 was abolished by pre-incubation of the antiserum with an excess of recombinant MDGA1-Fc antigen (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating antibody specificity through competition assay.

claim: The MDGA1 antiserum recognizes a single band around 130 kDa in brain homogenates from wild-type mice.
source: The MDGA1 antiserum recognized a single band around 130 kDa in brain homogenates from wild-type mice, which was not present in brain homogenates from Mdga1 KO mice, demonstrating antibody specificity (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating detection of endogenous MDGA1.

claim: The 130 kDa band detected by MDGA1 antiserum is absent in brain homogenates from Mdga1 KO mice.
source: The MDGA1 antiserum recognized a single band around 130 kDa in brain homogenates from wild-type mice, which was not present in brain homogenates from Mdga1 KO mice, demonstrating antibody specificity (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating antibody specificity through knockout validation.

claim: MDGA1 shows abundant localization in the hippocampus, with prominent labeling in CA3 and CA1 stratum radiatum and stratum oriens.
source: Immunohistochemistry on brain sections showed abundant MDGA1 localization in the hippocampus, with prominent labeling in CA3 and CA1 stratum radiatum and stratum oriens containing pyramidal neuron dendrites (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: MDGA1 staining was absent in brain sections from Mdga1 KO mice.
source: MDGA1 staining was absent in brain sections from Mdga1 KO mice (Ishikawa et al., 2011), showing antibody specificity in tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and citation to previous work establishing the knockout model.

claim: MDGA1 was detected in both pre-synaptic and post-synaptic fractions from synaptosome preparations.
source: MDGA1 was detected both in pre-synaptic and post-synaptic fractions from synaptosome preparations, revealing its presence in synaptic compartments (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Abundant levels of MDGA2 mRNAs were detected by RT-qPCR in hippocampal cultures.
source: However, we detected abundant levels of MDGA2 mRNAs by RT-qPCR in hippocampal cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B), in agreement with previous in situ hybridization and β-galactosidase staining (Connor et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2013), together suggesting that the MDGA2 protein is also expressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data and citations to previous studies.

claim: mRNAs for both MDGA1 and MDGA2 were detected in astrocyte cultures.
source: Interestingly, we also detected mRNAs for both MDGA1 and MDGA2 in astrocyte cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The fraction of excitatory post-synapses containing MDGA1 clusters was 45% at DIV 7.
source: Quantitatively, the fraction of excitatory post-synapses containing MDGA1 clusters was 45% and 40% at DIV 7 and 14, respectively, and decreased to 25% at DIV 21 (Figure 1G)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The fraction of excitatory post-synapses containing MDGA1 clusters was 40% at DIV 14.
source: Quantitatively, the fraction of excitatory post-synapses containing MDGA1 clusters was 45% and 40% at DIV 7 and 14, respectively, and decreased to 25% at DIV 21 (Figure 1G)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The fraction of excitatory post-synapses containing MDGA1 clusters decreased to 25% at DIV 21.
source: Quantitatively, the fraction of excitatory post-synapses containing MDGA1 clusters was 45% and 40% at DIV 7 and 14, respectively, and decreased to 25% at DIV 21 (Figure 1G)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The proportion of inhibitory post-synapses containing MDGA1 was 20% at DIV 10.
source: while the proportion of inhibitory post-synapses containing MDGA1 was 20% at DIV 10 and increased to 30% at DIV 14 and 21 (Figure 1J)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunostaining data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The proportion of inhibitory post-synapses containing MDGA1 increased to 30% at DIV 14 and 21.
source: while the proportion of inhibitory post-synapses containing MDGA1 was 20% at DIV 10 and increased to 30% at DIV 14 and 21 (Figure 1J)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunostaining data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: MDGA1 partially redistributes from excitatory to inhibitory synapses upon neuronal maturation.
source: Quantitatively, the fraction of excitatory post-synapses containing MDGA1 clusters was 45% and 40% at DIV 7 and 14, respectively, and decreased to 25% at DIV 21 (Figure 1G), while the proportion of inhibitory post-synapses containing MDGA1 was 20% at DIV 10 and increased to 30% at DIV 14 and 21 (Figure 1J), suggesting that MDGA1 partially redistributes from excitatory to inhibitory synapses upon neuronal maturation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed changes in MDGA1 localization at excitatory versus inhibitory synapses over time.

claim: The area overlap between PSD-95 and MDGA1 was around 15–30%.
source: Overall, among synapses that contained MDGA1, the area overlap between PSD-95 and MDGA1, or between gephyrin and MDGA1 was around 15–30% (Figure 1H and K), pointing to a minor occupancy of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses by MDGA1.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1H and K.

claim: The area overlap between gephyrin and MDGA1 was around 15–30%.
source: Overall, among synapses that contained MDGA1, the area overlap between PSD-95 and MDGA1, or between gephyrin and MDGA1 was around 15–30% (Figure 1H and K), pointing to a minor occupancy of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses by MDGA1.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1H and K.

claim: shMDGA1 caused a 75% decrease of surface MDGA1 immunofluorescence level compared with non-electroporated cells or cells expressing shCTRL.
source: In neurons, we measured a 75% decrease of surface MDGA1 immunofluorescence level in cells expressing shMDGA1 as compared with non-electroporated cells or cells expressing shCTRL (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,C.

claim: shMDGA2 caused a 40% reduction in mRNA level compared with shCTRL.
source: In neurons electroporated with shMDGA2, we estimated a 40% reduction in mRNA level as compared with shCTRL by RT-qPCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Neurons co-expressing shMDGA1 and rescue AP-MDGA1 showed a 1.5-fold increase in MDGA1 surface immunostaining compared to non-electroporated cells.
source: Neurons co-expressing shMDGA1 and rescue AP-MDGA1 showed a 1.5-fold increase in MDGA1 surface immunostaining compared to non-electroporated cells, reflecting a mild over-expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, D.

claim: AP-MDGA1 and AP-MDGA2 displayed a fairly uniform distribution at DIV 10 and 14, filling the whole dendritic shaft without specific accumulation at synapses.
source: Using this approach, AP-MDGA1 and AP-MDGA2 displayed a fairly uniform distribution at DIV 10 and 14, filling the whole dendritic shaft without specific accumulation at synapses, similarly to the negative control GFP-GPI (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by dSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 10 was around 1.3 for MDGA1.
source: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 10 and 14 was around 1.3 and 1.5 for both MDGAs and GFP-GPI, and significantly higher for NLGN1 (2.3 and 2.7, respectively) (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 14 was around 1.5 for MDGA1.
source: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 10 and 14 was around 1.3 and 1.5 for both MDGAs and GFP-GPI, and significantly higher for NLGN1 (2.3 and 2.7, respectively) (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 10 was around 1.3 for MDGA2.
source: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 10 and 14 was around 1.3 and 1.5 for both MDGAs and GFP-GPI, and significantly higher for NLGN1 (2.3 and 2.7, respectively) (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 14 was around 1.5 for MDGA2.
source: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 10 and 14 was around 1.3 and 1.5 for both MDGAs and GFP-GPI, and significantly higher for NLGN1 (2.3 and 2.7, respectively) (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 10 was 2.3 for NLGN1.
source: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 10 and 14 was around 1.3 and 1.5 for both MDGAs and GFP-GPI, and significantly higher for NLGN1 (2.3 and 2.7, respectively) (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 14 was 2.7 for NLGN1.
source: Synaptic enrichment at DIV 10 and 14 was around 1.3 and 1.5 for both MDGAs and GFP-GPI, and significantly higher for NLGN1 (2.3 and 2.7, respectively) (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dSTORM data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Biotinylated AP-MDGA1 strongly recruits HA-NLGN1 in streptavidin pull-down experiments.
source: Streptavidin pull-down of proteins extracted from COS-7 cells expressing AP-MDGA1, BirAER, and HA-NLGN1, followed by anti-MDGA1 and anti-NLGN1 immunoblots, revealed that biotinylated AP-MDGA1 strongly recruits HA-NLGN1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by biochemical pull-down data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: At DIV 8, recombinant AP-MDGA1 diffused very fast in the dendritic membrane, showing a single peak of diffusion coefficient around 0.30 µm²/s.
source: At DIV 8, recombinant AP-MDGA1 and AP-MDGA2 diffused very fast in the dendritic membrane, showing a single peak of diffusion coefficient around 0.30 µm²/s, very similar to GFP-GPI (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: At DIV 8, recombinant AP-MDGA2 diffused very fast in the dendritic membrane, showing a single peak of diffusion coefficient around 0.30 µm²/s.
source: At DIV 8, recombinant AP-MDGA1 and AP-MDGA2 diffused very fast in the dendritic membrane, showing a single peak of diffusion coefficient around 0.30 µm²/s, very similar to GFP-GPI (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The median diffusion coefficient of MDGA1 and MDGA2 at DIV 8 was around 0.13–0.15 µm²/s.
source: Considering a small fraction (around 20%) of slowly mobile molecules, defined as molecules exploring an area smaller than the pointing accuracy of the optical system, i.e. D < 0.01 µm²/s (Chamma et al., 2016a), the median diffusion coefficient of the overall distribution was around 0.13–0.15 µm²/s across conditions (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 3G and H, with citation to previous methodology.

claim: Upon neuronal maturation (at DIV 10 and 14), the fraction of slowly mobile molecules increased for MDGA1 and MDGA2.
source: Upon neuronal maturation (at DIV 10 and 14), the fraction of slowly mobile molecules increased for MDGA1 and MDGA2, with a concomitant decrease in median diffusion coefficient, while those parameters remained fairly constant for GFP-GPI (Figure 3C–H), suggesting a specific immobilization of MDGAs at these developmental stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 3C–H.

claim: Upon neuronal maturation (at DIV 10 and 14), there was a concomitant decrease in median diffusion coefficient for MDGA1 and MDGA2.
source: Upon neuronal maturation (at DIV 10 and 14), the fraction of slowly mobile molecules increased for MDGA1 and MDGA2, with a concomitant decrease in median diffusion coefficient, while those parameters remained fairly constant for GFP-GPI (Figure 3C–H), suggesting a specific immobilization of MDGAs at these developmental stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 3C–H.

claim: The fraction of slowly mobile molecules and median diffusion coefficient remained fairly constant for GFP-GPI across DIV 8, 10, and 14.
source: Upon neuronal maturation (at DIV 10 and 14), the fraction of slowly mobile molecules increased for MDGA1 and MDGA2, with a concomitant decrease in median diffusion coefficient, while those parameters remained fairly constant for GFP-GPI (Figure 3C–H), suggesting a specific immobilization of MDGAs at these developmental stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 3C–H.

claim: Synaptic coverage of MDGA1 was only 20% at both DIV 10 and 14.
source: Synaptic coverage of MDGA1 and MDGA2 was only 20% at both DIV 10 and 14, while it reached 40% for GFP-GPI, indicating that MDGAs dynamically explore only a minor fraction of the synaptic cleft.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of uPAINT data shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: Synaptic coverage of MDGA2 was only 20% at both DIV 10 and 14.
source: Synaptic coverage of MDGA1 and MDGA2 was only 20% at both DIV 10 and 14, while it reached 40% for GFP-GPI, indicating that MDGAs dynamically explore only a minor fraction of the synaptic cleft.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of uPAINT data shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: Synaptic coverage of GFP-GPI reached 40% at DIV 10 and 14.
source: Synaptic coverage of MDGA1 and MDGA2 was only 20% at both DIV 10 and 14, while it reached 40% for GFP-GPI, indicating that MDGAs dynamically explore only a minor fraction of the synaptic cleft.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of uPAINT data shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: At DIV 10, a 2.5-fold increase in the density of Homer1c-DsRed puncta was observed in neurons expressing shMDGA2 relatively to shCTRL.
source: At DIV 10, a 2.5-fold increase in the density of Homer1c-DsRed puncta was observed in neurons expressing shMDGA2 relatively to shCTRL, whereas no significant effect of shMDGA1 was observed on the density of excitatory post-synaptic clusters (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: At DIV 10, no significant effect of shMDGA1 was observed on the density of excitatory post-synaptic clusters.
source: At DIV 10, a 2.5-fold increase in the density of Homer1c-DsRed puncta was observed in neurons expressing shMDGA2 relatively to shCTRL, whereas no significant effect of shMDGA1 was observed on the density of excitatory post-synaptic clusters (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: At DIV 14, both shMDGA1 and shMDGA2 induced a modest 25% increase in the density of post-synaptic puncta.
source: At DIV 14, both shMDGA1 and shMDGA2 induced a modest 25% increase in the density of post-synaptic puncta (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D), suggesting an attenuation of the effect at later developmental stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: In DIV 10 neurons, shMDGA2 had no effect on the NLGN1 diffusion coefficient.
source: In DIV 10 neurons, shMDGA2 had no effect on the NLGN1 diffusion coefficient, whose distribution looked very similar to the shCTRL condition (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: At DIV 14, shMDGA2 decreased the global diffusion coefficient of NLGN1 as compared to shCTRL.
source: In contrast, at DIV 14, shMDGA2 decreased the global diffusion coefficient of NLGN1 as compared to shCTRL, in particular by reducing the mobile pool of NLGN1 molecules (the peak centered at D = 0.1 µm²/s), and concomitantly raising the fraction of confined NLGN1 molecules (peak at D = 0.01 µm²/s) that are most likely retained at synapses (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 5E–H.

claim: The effect of shMDGA2 on NLGN1 diffusion at DIV 14 was reversed upon the co-expression of an HA-MDGA2 construct resistant to shMDGA2.
source: This effect was reversed upon the co-expression of an HA-MDGA2 construct resistant to shMDGA2.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5E–H.

claim: In DIV 10 neurons, there was no significant effect of shMDGA2 on NLGN1 enrichment at Homer1c-DsRed positive puncta compared to shCTRL.
source: In DIV 10 neurons, there was no significant effect of shMDGA2 on NLGN1 enrichment at Homer1c-DsRed positive puncta compared to shCTRL (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by dSTORM data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: In DIV 14 neurons, an increase from 3 to 4 in the synaptic enrichment of AP-NLGN1 was observed upon shMDGA2 expression as compared to shCTRL, albeit not significant.
source: In DIV 14 neurons, an increase from 3 to 4 in the synaptic enrichment of AP-NLGN1 was observed upon shMDGA2 expression as compared to shCTRL, albeit not significant (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by dSTORM data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The NLGN phosphotyrosine level was almost two-fold higher in neurons expressing shMDGA2 compared to shCTRL at DIV 10.
source: The NLGN phosphotyrosine level was almost two-fold higher in neurons expressing shMDGA2 compared to shCTRL, with no change in the total amount of NLGNs (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data shown in Figure 6E–G.

claim: There was no change in the total amount of NLGNs in neurons expressing shMDGA2 compared to shCTRL.
source: The NLGN phosphotyrosine level was almost two-fold higher in neurons expressing shMDGA2 compared to shCTRL, with no change in the total amount of NLGNs (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data shown in Figure 6E–G.

claim: Expression of shMDGA2 significantly decreased the global AMPAR diffusion coefficient at DIV 10 compared to shCTRL.
source: Expression of shMDGA2 significantly decreased the global AMPAR diffusion coefficient at DIV 10 compared to shCTRL (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 7A–D.

claim: At DIV 14, expression of shMDGA2 caused a further small decrease in AMPAR diffusion coefficient.
source: At DIV 14, the distribution of AMPAR diffusion coefficients was shifted to the left as compared to DIV 10, reflecting AMPAR trapping at new synapses formed during this time interval (Figure 7E–H). Expression of shMDGA2 caused a further small decrease in diffusion coefficient, matching the observation that neurons expressing shMDGA2 show slightly higher numbers of excitatory synapses at DIV 14 as compared to neurons expressing shCTRL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-molecule tracking data shown in Figure 7E–H.

claim: At DIV 10, an almost doubling in the number of PSD-95 puncta per unit dendrite length was observed in neurons expressing gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 relatively to control gRNA.
source: At DIV 10, an almost doubling in the number of PSD-95 puncta per unit dendrite length without a change in PSD-95 area, was observed in neurons expressing gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 relatively to control gRNA (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8A–C.

claim: At DIV 10, there was no change in PSD-95 area in neurons expressing gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 relatively to control gRNA.
source: At DIV 10, an almost doubling in the number of PSD-95 puncta per unit dendrite length without a change in PSD-95 area, was observed in neurons expressing gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 relatively to control gRNA (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8A–C.

claim: At DIV 10, only gRNA to MDGA2 caused a significant increase in the density of VGLUT1 puncta.
source: In the same conditions, only gRNA to MDGA2 caused a significant increase in the density of VGLUT1 puncta, and no change in area (Figure 8A, D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8A, D and E.

claim: At DIV 10, gRNA to MDGA2 caused no change in VGLUT1 puncta area.
source: In the same conditions, only gRNA to MDGA2 caused a significant increase in the density of VGLUT1 puncta, and no change in area (Figure 8A, D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8A, D and E.

claim: The effects of gRNA to MDGA2 on both PSD-95 and VGLUT1 cluster density were abolished by the co-expression of a rescue MDGA2 vector.
source: Those effects of gRNA to MDGA2 on both PSD-95 and VGLUT1 cluster density were abolished by the co-expression of a rescue MDGA2 vector, demonstrating the specificity of the mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 8.

claim: At DIV 14, gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 did not change PSD-95 cluster density or area relative to control gRNA.
source: At DIV 14, gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 did not change PSD-95 cluster density or area relative to control gRNA, but slightly decreased both VGLUT1 puncta density and area (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: At DIV 14, gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 slightly decreased both VGLUT1 puncta density and area.
source: At DIV 14, gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 did not change PSD-95 cluster density or area relative to control gRNA, but slightly decreased both VGLUT1 puncta density and area (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: No effects of CRISPR-Cas9 combined with either gRNA to MDGA1 or MDGA2 were found on the density or the area of gephyrin puncta at DIV 10.
source: In contrast, no effects of CRISPR-Cas9 combined with either gRNA to MDGA1 or MDGA2 were found on the density or the area of gephyrin puncta at DIV 10 (Figure 8—figure supplement 4A-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4A-C.

claim: Neurons expressing gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 showed a threefold increase in the frequency of AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs compared with neurons expressing control gRNA.
source: Neurons expressing gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 showed a threefold increase in the frequency of AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs compared with neurons expressing control gRNA, while the combined expression of gRNA to MDGA2 and rescue MDGA2 abolished this effect (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8F and G.

claim: The combined expression of gRNA to MDGA2 and rescue MDGA2 abolished the increase in AMPAR-mediated mEPSC frequency.
source: Neurons expressing gRNAs to MDGA1 or MDGA2 showed a threefold increase in the frequency of AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs compared with neurons expressing control gRNA, while the combined expression of gRNA to MDGA2 and rescue MDGA2 abolished this effect (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8F and G.

claim: No significant change in the amplitude of AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs was observed across conditions (CRISPR CTRL, MDGA1, MDGA2).
source: No significant change in the amplitude of AMPAR-mediated mEPSCs was observed across conditions (Figure 8H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: No significant change in either the frequency or amplitude of mIPSCs was observed upon single-cell KO of MDGA1 or MDGA2.
source: In contrast, no significant change in either the frequency or amplitude of mIPSCs was observed upon single-cell KO of MDGA1 or MDGA2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 4D-F), suggesting that MDGAs do not affect inhibitory synapse formation during this developmental period.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4D-F.

claim: Both gRNAs to MDGA1 and MDGA2 increased AMPAR-mediated EPSCs without affecting NMDAR-mediated EPSCs in organotypic slices.
source: Strikingly, both gRNAs to MDGA1 and MDGA2 increased AMPAR-mediated EPSCs without affecting NMDAR-mediated EPSCs, as compared to non-electroporated controls (Figure 9B-D and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 9B-D and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The ratio between AMPAR- and NMDAR-mediated EPSCs was significantly elevated in both MDGA1 and MDGA2 KO neurons in organotypic slices.
source: As a result, the ratio between AMPAR- and NMDAR-mediated EPSCs was significantly elevated in both MDGA1 and MDGA2 KO neurons (Figure 9E), supporting a synaptic unsilencing mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: No significant effect of gRNA CTRL on either AMPAR- or NMDAR-mediated EPSCs, or on the AMPA/NMDA ratio was observed when compared to non-electroporated neurons.
source: No significant effect of gRNA CTRL on either AMPAR- or NMDAR-mediated EPSCs, or on the AMPA/NMDA ratio was observed when compared to non-electroporated neurons (Figure 9B-E), validating the normalization procedure and the absence of off-target effects of the control gRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 9B-E.

claim: No effect of CRISPR to MDGA1 or MDGA2 on the paired-pulse ratio was observed.
source: No effect of CRISPR to MDGA1 or MDGA2 on the paired-pulse ratio was observed (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C, D), ruling out pre-synaptic mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: MDGAs are essentially non-synaptically enriched molecules that exhibit fast diffusion in the dendritic membrane.
source: In this study, we characterized the membrane localization of MDGAs and their role on the dynamics and signaling of their direct binding partner, NLGN1, as well as associated effects on synaptic differentiation and the recruitment of AMPARs. We demonstrate that both MDGA1 and MDGA2 are essentially non-synaptically enriched molecules that exhibit fast diffusion in the dendritic membrane.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from multiple experiments in the study.

claim: The knock-down of MDGAs selectively increases excitatory synapse density.
source: Moreover, the knock-down of MDGAs selectively increases excitatory synapse density and as a consequence reduces the surface mobility of both NLGN1 and AMPARs, increases AMPAR-mediated mEPSC frequency and evoked EPSC amplitude, as well as NLGN1 phosphosignaling.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from multiple experiments in the study.

claim: The knock-down of MDGAs reduces the surface mobility of both NLGN1 and AMPARs.
source: Moreover, the knock-down of MDGAs selectively increases excitatory synapse density and as a consequence reduces the surface mobility of both NLGN1 and AMPARs, increases AMPAR-mediated mEPSC frequency and evoked EPSC amplitude, as well as NLGN1 phosphosignaling.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from multiple experiments in the study.

claim: The knock-down of MDGAs increases AMPAR-mediated mEPSC frequency.
source: Moreover, the knock-down of MDGAs selectively increases excitatory synapse density and as a consequence reduces the surface mobility of both NLGN1 and AMPARs, increases AMPAR-mediated mEPSC frequency and evoked EPSC amplitude, as well as NLGN1 phosphosignaling.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from multiple experiments in the study.

claim: The knock-down of MDGAs increases evoked EPSC amplitude.
source: Moreover, the knock-down of MDGAs selectively increases excitatory synapse density and as a consequence reduces the surface mobility of both NLGN1 and AMPARs, increases AMPAR-mediated mEPSC frequency and evoked EPSC amplitude, as well as NLGN1 phosphosignaling.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from multiple experiments in the study.

claim: The knock-down of MDGAs increases NLGN1 phosphosignaling.
source: Moreover, the knock-down of MDGAs selectively increases excitatory synapse density and as a consequence reduces the surface mobility of both NLGN1 and AMPARs, increases AMPAR-mediated mEPSC frequency and evoked EPSC amplitude, as well as NLGN1 phosphosignaling.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings from multiple experiments in the study.

claim: By shielding a fraction of NLGN1 from binding to pre-synaptic NRXNs, MDGAs negatively regulate NLGN function in excitatory synaptic differentiation.
source: Thus, by shielding a fraction of NLGN1 from binding to pre-synaptic NRXNs, MDGAs negatively regulates NLGN function in excitatory synaptic differentiation (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental findings and supported by the model in Figure 10.

claim: NLGN1 is primarily localized at excitatory synapses.
source: Neuroligins (NLGNs) are post-synaptic proteins that comprise four members in rodents (NLGN1-4), NLGN1 being primarily localized at excitatory synapses, NLGN2 and NLGN4 at inhibitory synapses, and NLGN3 at both types of synapses (Budreck and Scheiffele, 2007; Varoqueaux et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NLGN3 is localized at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NLGNs form both homo- and hetero-dimers through cis-interactions between their acetylcholinesterase (AchE)-like domains.
source: At the structural level, NLGNs form both homo- and hetero-dimers through cis-interactions between their acetylcholinesterase (AchE)-like domains (Araç et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2008; Dean et al., 2003; Fabrichny et al., 2007; Poulopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: MDGAs were reported to bind in cis to NLGNs with high affinity and compete with their binding to NRXNs.
source: Recently, MAM-domain GPI-anchored molecules (MDGAs) were reported to bind in cis to NLGNs with high affinity and compete with their binding to NRXNs (Connor et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The expression of MDGAs together with NLGNs in heterologous cells impairs the synapse-inducing activity of NLGNs on contacting axons in the co-culture assay.
source: In the co-culture assay, the expression of MDGAs together with NLGNs in heterologous cells impairs the synapse-inducing activity of NLGNs on contacting axons (Elegheert et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2013; Pettem et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Crystal structures of MDGA-NLGN complexes revealed that MDGAs bind through their first Ig1-Ig2 domains to the two lobes of the NLGN extracellular dimer, at sites which overlap with the NRXN binding interface.
source: Crystal structures of MDGA-NLGN complexes revealed that MDGAs bind through their first Ig1-Ig2 domains to the two lobes of the NLGN extracellular dimer, at sites which overlap with the NRXN binding interface (Elegheert et al., 2017; Gangwar et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: MDGA1 selectively inhibits inhibitory synapse formation by primarily repressing NLGN2-NRXN interactions.
source: Manipulations of MDGA1 protein levels by over-expression (OE), knock-down (KD), or knock-out (KO) in neurons have led to the common view that MDGA1 selectively inhibits inhibitory synapse formation by primarily repressing NLGN2-NRXN interactions (Connor et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2013; Loh et al., 2016; Pettem et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MDGA2 KO specifically inhibits excitatory synapse formation in vivo.
source: Similar studies performed on MDGA2 have led to more debated results, i.e. some reports showing that MDGA2 KO specifically inhibits excitatory synapse formation in vivo (Connor et al., 2016), while others showing no effect of MDGA2 KD on either excitatory or inhibitory synapses in culture (Loh et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.
